text: {He} had the look of a {man} who had never once been asked to pay for anything at the time.
{He} had the good coat and the bad posture of somebody waiting for the family money to arrive by itself.
{He} had the easy manners of somebody who has been forgiven for everything so far and expects the streak to hold.
{He} had the look of a {man} who kept the good china for company and had decided I wasn’t company.
{He} held {his} handbag on {his} knees with both hands, and I got the feeling it had heard worse than me.
{He} sat very straight, in case the avenue was watching, and on the avenue somebody always is.
{He} had the look of somebody who could sell you a share of anything, including the hat on your head.
{He} kept one eye on me and the other on the door, in case a better customer came through it.
{He} had the quick, pleasant face of a {man} who has never once let anybody see {him} count.
{He} had the look of a {man} who could make a party sound wonderful without having enjoyed a minute of it.
{He} looked me over and decided which paragraph I’d go in, and it wasn’t the first one.
{He} had good gloves, a sharp pencil, and the patient smile of somebody who gets paid by the name.
{He} had the look of a {man} who knew what every window on the street was paying and which ones were late.
{He} took up a good deal of the room and had the air of somebody who owned the floor under it, which {he} probably did.
{He} had a landlord’s face: sympathetic right up to the first of the month.
{He} had the look of a {man} who charged by the quarter hour and had just started counting mine.
{He} listened with {his} head on one side, weighing whether anything I said would stand up in court.
{He} had the tidy, underfed look of a lawyer with one clerk and a great many opinions about the clerk.
{He} had the look of a {man} who could find a missing nickel in a year of books and tell you which day it went.
{He} sat with {his} elbows in, from twenty years at a desk too small for {him}.
{He} had ink on one finger and the kind of patience that comes from adding the same column three times.
{He} had the look of a {man} who has heard every excuse a sick man can make and believes none of them.
{He} looked me over with professional interest and found nothing worth a thermometer.
{He} had very clean cuffs and the calm of somebody who stays up all night on purpose, and for money.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had bought {his} practice second-hand and was still paying off the chair.
{He} had the steady hands of somebody who tells people it won’t hurt for a living, and the eyes of somebody who knows better.
{He} watched my mouth while I talked, which is a professional habit and not a comfortable one.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had typed other people’s secrets for years and never once hit the wrong key.
{He} sat with {his} hands folded, ready for somebody to walk in and dictate a letter.
{He} had a pencil behind one ear and the air of somebody who had already filed me under a heading.
{He} had the look of a {man} who would put me in the evening edition if I said anything worth a paragraph.
{He} had a pencil out before I’d got my hat off, which told me who thought this was an interview.
{He} had the rumpled, hungry look of somebody paid by the line and short of lines this week.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had sat through ten thousand scales and forgiven about half of them.
{He} kept time on {his} knee with two fingers without knowing it, which is either music or nerves.
{He} had the patient, faintly pained face of somebody who listens to children practise for a living.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had never once believed a fire started by itself.
{He} looked around the room and priced it, in case it burned down while we talked.
{He} had a pleasant face and a doubtful mind, which in {his} line counts as a uniform.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had made a thousand beds and knew exactly what got left in them.
{He} stood half ready to be rung for, and hoping nobody would.
{He} had red hands and sharp eyes, and I’d have bet the eyes did more of the work.
{He} had the look of a {man} who picked up heavy things for a living and put them down only when paid.
{He} had shoulders wide enough to need their own chair.
{He} had big scarred hands folded on the table, and {he} kept them there, which I appreciated.
{He} had the look of a {man} who could tell you what my coat cost and how much of that was a lie.
{He} had pins in {his} lapel and a squint from close work, and {he} used the squint on me.
{He} kept smoothing a fold in {his} sleeve that wasn’t there, which is what happens when your hands are never off the clock.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had driven every street in the city and had a complaint about each of them.
{He} had {his} cap pushed back and the patience of somebody who gets paid to wait.
{He} sat with one arm along the back of the seat, a {man} expecting a fare and getting me.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had measured me for a better suit the moment I came in.
{He} had a tape measure round {his} neck and no intention of taking it off for me.
{He} glanced at my cuffs, winced, and was too polite to say anything, which was worse.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had moved a great deal of scenery and been thanked by none of it.
{He} had rope burns on both palms and the unbothered face of somebody who works where nobody looks.
{He} stood with {his} weight back, ready to catch something falling, which in {his} line is most things.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had heard half the neighbourhood’s business and been asked to forget all of it.
{He} sat up straight, still listening for a light to come on over the next line.
{He} had a pleasant, careful voice that sounded rehearsed, because {he} had used it forty times an hour all day.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had seen every guest come in late and heard every reason why.
{He} had a carnation in {his} buttonhole that had been fresh this afternoon and was now just loyal.
{He} was polite to me with the practised politeness of somebody who is polite to everybody and remembers who tipped.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had kicked in a line of twenty and could tell you which of the other nineteen were half a step late.
{He} was between engagements and dressed for the next one, just in case it walked in.
{He} had stage paint still at the hairline and the bright, tired smile of somebody who does two shows a night.
{He} had the look of a {man} who would give you odds on anything, including whether I’d get anything out of {him}.
{He} had chalk on {his} cuff and a pencil stub behind {his} ear, and neither of them had ever lost money.
{He} was friendly, with the friendliness of a {man} who knows exactly what you owe {him}.
{He} had the look of a {man} who knew every voter on the block and what each of them wanted for Christmas.
{He} shook my hand before I’d offered it, which is how you can tell the ones who work for the club.
{He} had a big warm smile that stopped a good inch short of {his} eyes.
{He} had the look of a {man} who could tell you what anything was worth, and what you’d take for it.
{He} looked at my watch before {he} looked at me, and {he} wasn’t impressed by either.
{He} had the pale, patient face of somebody who spends the day behind a grille hearing why things have to go.
{He} had the look of a {man} whose whole job was standing in a doorway being larger than the doorway.
{He} cracked {his} knuckles one at a time, not at me exactly, but in my general direction.
{He} had a nose that had been broken at least twice and an expression that said the other fellows had it worse.
{He} had the look of a {man} who could remember forty numbers and forty names and forget any of them for a price.
{He} kept glancing at the street, which in {his} line is the same as breathing.
{He} had quick feet, quick eyes, and a jacket with more inside pockets than a jacket needs.
{He} had the look of a {man} who knew what I drank before I did and wasn’t going to say it out loud.
{He} kept wiping the same spot on the bar, which had been clean since the last election.
{He} had the mild, deaf expression bartenders wear when a customer is about to tell them something.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had opened ten thousand doors and was keeping count of who tipped.
{He} had a uniform with more brass on it than the average general, and {he} knew it.
{He} stood very still, with the special knack doormen have for being furniture until somebody needs them.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had read every paper in the stand and believed none of them.
{He} made change without looking at it, which in {his} line is the only skill that matters.
{He} had newsprint on {his} fingers and the whole neighbourhood’s business somewhere behind {his} eyes.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had poured a million cups of coffee and been thanked for about six.
{He} leaned on {his} counter with the calm of somebody who owns the only warm room on the block.
{He} had a pencil behind {his} ear for orders and no intention of writing mine down.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had torn a hundred thousand tickets in half and enjoyed maybe three.
{He} looked at me for a ticket stub first and a face second.
{He} had the glassy patience of somebody who has watched the same picture forty times from the lobby.
{He} had the look of a {man} who went up and down all day and had strong opinions about both.
{He} knew every tenant by the floor they got off at, and I could see {him} trying to work out mine.
{He} had white gloves and the gravity of a {man} trusted with the only lift in the building.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had heard every excuse for late rent and kept a drawer for each of them.
{He} sat where {he} could see the stairs, and I realised that included me.
{He} counted everything, and I got the feeling I was being counted too.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had walked the same streets for years and had a favourite doorway on every one of them.
{He} had cold ears, warm boots, and the settled face of somebody who gets paid whether anything happens or not.
{He} rocked on {his} heels and considered me, which is what they teach them instead of manners.
{He} had the look of a {man} who had sat in the same seat so long it had given up and taken {his} shape.
{He} had the radio going low and an opinion about every fare of the evening.
{He} looked at me in the mirror first, from habit, before turning round.
{He} had the look of a {man} who knew what everybody on the street was taking and why.
{He} peered at me over {his} spectacles with the caution of somebody who has to sign for things.
{He} had a clean white coat and a quiet voice that {he} never raised above the price of aspirin.
{He} had the look of somebody who had been having a long night before I got there.
{He} looked at me with the polite dread people keep for detectives and dentists.
{He} had a face that was trying hard to look as if it had nothing to do with anything.
{He} gave me the same look as before, only less of it.
{He} didn’t sigh, but {he} let me watch {him} decide not to.
{He} waited, which with {him} was most of the conversation.
{He} had the patient look of somebody being asked for directions twice.
{He} settled in for another one, without much joy.
{He} looked at me, then at the clock, and decided I was still there.
{He} brightened, which is what that kind does when you come back.
{He} had been hoping I’d ask something else, and it showed.
{He} leaned in, glad of the company.
{He} gave me the look people give the second question, which is less polite than the one they give the first.
{He} put down what {he} was doing, again.
